etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English mob, short for mobile, from Latin mōbile (vulgus) (“fickle (crowd)”). The video-gaming sense originates from English mobile, used by Richard Bartle for objects capable of movement in an early MUD.

definitions.definition: A large or disorderly group of people; especially one bent on riotous or destructive action.

quote.citation: February 13, 1788, James Madison, Jr., Federalist No. 55
quote.text: Had every Athenian citizen been a Socrates, every Athenian assembly would still have been a mob.

definitions.definition: (archaic) The lower classes of a community; the rabble.

quote.citation: 1715 June 1 (Gregorian calendar), Joseph Addison, “The Free-holder: No. 44. Saturday, May 21. [1715.]”, in The Works of the Right Honourable Joseph Addison, Esq; […], volume IV, London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], published 1721, →OCLC:
quote.text: A cluster of mob, who were making themselves merry with their betters.

definitions.definition: (collective noun) A group of animals such as horses or cattle.
A mafia: a group that engages in organized crime.

quote.citation: 1920, Mary Roberts Rinehart, Avery Hopwood, chapter I, in The Bat: A Novel from the Play (Dell Book; 241), New York, N.Y.: Dell Publishing Company, →OCLC, page 01:
quote.text: The Bat—they called him the Bat. […]. He'd never been in stir, the bulls had never mugged him, he didn't run with a mob, he played a lone hand, and fenced his stuff so that even the fence couldn't swear he knew his face.

quote.citation: 1986, Paul Chadwick, Concrete: Under the Desert Stars, Dark Horse Books:
quote.text: What if it is a mob killing? They can’t hurt me, but …

See also: Mafia (proper noun senses for specific ones)

definitions.definition: (Australian Aboriginal) A group of Aboriginal people associated with an extended family group, clan group or wider community group, from a particular place or country.[1]

quote.citation: 2011 March 10, Allan Clarke, W.A. through Noongar eyes‎[1]:
quote.text: There’s nothing like local knowledge and after thousands of years living here the Noongar mob understand this land better than anyone, so it makes sense for them to tap into the lucrative tourism industry.

quote.citation: 2021 November 7, Claire [G.] Coleman, “Not quite blak enough: ‘The people who think I am too white to be Aboriginal are all white’”, in The Guardian‎[2]:
quote.text: There’s a saying among blak mob, ‘It doesn’t matter how much milk you put in tea, it’s still tea.’ I am a descendant of genocide survivors, a child of the oldest living culture on Earth. Nothing, no amount of milk, can change that.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To crowd around (someone), sometimes with hostility.

quote.citation: 2017 June 26, Alexis Petridis, “Glastonbury 2017 verdict: Radiohead, Foo Fighters, Lorde, Stormzy and more”, in the Guardian‎[3]:
quote.text: Politicians have been turning up to Glastonbury for years, but this year the leader of the opposition was among the most hotly anticipated attractions: when he arrived on site, his Land Rover was mobbed by fans.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To crowd into or around a place.
(obsolete) A promiscuous woman; a harlot or wench; a prostitute. [17th–18th c.]

quote.citation: c. 1773-1774, Oliver Goldsmith, letter to Mrs Bunbury

definitions.definition: (transitive) To wrap up in, or cover with, a cowl.
(video games) A non-player character, especially one that exists to be fought or killed to further the progression of the story or game.

quote.citation: 2002, Wolfie, “Re: Whoa - massive changes due in next patch”, in alt.games.everquest (Usenet):
quote.text: You can't win with small, balanced groups. You have to zerg the mob with a high number of players.
